description: We're Kavya and Shubh from Surat. We love turning raw NASA data into tools people can use: strong in Python, data analysis and web dashboards. We're tackling Lunar Landing Site Navigator, predicting sunlight and Earth contact at lunar south-pole sites with real NASA terrain data. Join us for serious science and a team that aims to win. Looking for: UI/UX design, video editing and storytelling, presenting, and any space science background.
summary:
Near the Moon's south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a ridge kilometres away can end a lander's day hours before a flat-horizon calculation says it will. Existing tools give a Sun angle. They don't say which ridge ends the light, or how far to trust the time.

Lunar Landing Site Navigator builds a 720-ray terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation data and NAIF SPICE geometry. Pick one of 23 sites (including 6 Artemis III candidate regions and 5 past landers) or type your own coordinates. It counts down to the next terrain sunset and Earth-set, names the ridge responsible, compares sites side by side and shows what a 2 m or 10 m mast gains. Where NASA DEM error clones exist (Shackleton rim, Connecting Ridge C1) it gives a P10–P90 range on the time.

We tested it against independent answers: JPL Horizons (largest error 0.002″), NASA PGDA illumination maps (Sun RMSE 2.84 percentage points over 60 points) and real missions. Blue Ghost 1 went dark 4.6 h after our predicted sunset, on battery. At the Chandrayaan-3 site a flat-horizon tool would put sunset 10.4 h later than the terrain does. It runs in a browser from one link.
details:
What it does

Pick a landing site, or type any coordinates south of 60°N. For that spot the navigator shows the Sun and Earth above the real terrain horizon, a countdown to the next terrain sunset and Earth-set (next to the time a flat-horizon tool would give), and which ridge causes it, named from the IAU gazetteer ("near Henson crater, 8.1 km away"). It adds 18.6-year illumination and Earth-visibility statistics, a stay planner, side-by-side site comparison, mast-height effects (0 / 2 / 10 m), CSV export, and replays of real mission endings: Chandrayaan-3, Blue Ghost 1, IM-1, IM-2 and SLIM.

How it works

  • Geometry: NAIF SPICE (DE440 ephemeris, Moon ME frame) for Sun and Earth directions.
  • Terrain: NASA LOLA polar DEMs from Goddard's PGDA and SLDEM2015 (LOLA + Kaguya), read with HTTP range requests, so no full downloads.
  • Horizon: 720 rays out to 100 km. The event search finds terrain sunset/sunrise and Earth-set/rise, and the ray that blocks the Sun gives the ridge's distance and name.
  • Uncertainty: 100 NASA DEM error clones (PGDA) give a P10–P90 time range at Shackleton rim and Connecting Ridge C1.
  • Delivery: a Python engine (FastAPI on Vercel) answers custom points live; curated sites are precomputed JSON; the dashboard is React + TypeScript.

How we checked it

Every number is reproducible with pytest and shown on the dashboard's Evidence tab.

  • Sun/Earth directions vs JPL Horizons: largest error 0.002″.
  • Illumination map vs NASA PGDA product 69, 60 points: Sun RMSE 2.84 percentage points, Earth RMSE 0.84.
  • Long-term illumination vs Gläser et al. 2018: Shackleton rim 80.2 % vs 81.0 %.
  • Mission endings: Blue Ghost 1 went dark 4.6 h after our predicted sunset (Firefly: its batteries lasted about 5 h). Chandrayaan-3 was put to sleep with the Sun still up, 4.7 h before our predicted terrain sunset; a flat horizon would put that sunset 10.4 h later still.
  • Negative controls: IM-1 and IM-2 ended for other reasons (orientation and power), so we report them and don't claim them.
    Presentation Deck: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PCsqhSVQfpQ7hqa6B1-ZofWeWVbdeTlc/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=105757536639441910258&rtpof=true&sd=true

Benefits and impact

One link replaces 12–18 clicks in LROC QuickMap to get a terrain-aware answer. It says which ridge ends the light and how sure the time is, and flags when a flat-horizon answer would be wrong by hours. Mission planners, students and space fans can check power and communication windows at a candidate site before committing to it.

GitHub: https://github.com/KavYaDesai2506/lunar-landing-site-navigator

What makes it different

It names the ridge, puts an error bar on the time where NASA's error data allow, and grades itself against real lander outcomes, including the cases it doesn't explain.

Tools

Python 3.13 (numpy, spiceypy, rasterio, FastAPI, pytest), TypeScript, React, Vite, Vercel, GitHub.

Limits

North polar region (60°N and above) is not supported yet. Uncertainty bands exist for 2 sites; others show a single best estimate. Lander orientation and solar-panel geometry are not modelled.

Use of SI

We used Anthropic's Claude for code, dashboard design, documentation drafts and research.
